subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to Hon. Members from all Parties. I just heard the unfortunate speech of the Hon. Member for Gander-[DOT] Twillingate (Mr. Baker), who decided to interject with political rhetoric about a vital issue.
He brought the level of debate down to a new low with his typical "Twillingate-isms" from Newfoundland. It is unfortunate that he could not have used the same style and quality as the Member from the New Democratic Party.
My concern about this issue of humane traps relates to my lifetime of outdoor interests. It goes back to 1974-79, during the period that I served on the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. At that time the Standing Committee had the opportunity, on an annual basis, to review the report of the Federal-Provincial Committee for the Development of Humane Trapping and the development of a humane trap. That committee was a creature of the Liberal
Government. It laboured long and hard to invite the trappers of Canada to send in their inventions for a humane trap and have those inventions tested.
This is now operated by the Fur Institute of Canada. The traps are now tested in Vegreville, Alberta, at the Environmental Research Centre run by the Alberta Government. Therein lies one of the problems which we face. The annual budget for the research centre at Vegreville is around $600,000. I suggest that if this nation has the capacity to put into space on a U.S. space vehicle something that is so vastly advanced in technology as the Canadarm, surely we have the inventiveness and the funds to develop a very precise and effective 100 per cent, "no problem whatsoever", humane trap.
In the minds of trappers there are, of course, precise traps for precise purposes for precise animals. In the minds of average persons, for example someone living on Bay Street or Bloor Street in Toronto, or anywhere else in a big city in Canada, a trap is a trap and an animal is an animal. They really do not make any differentiation as to how an animal is caught and how it dies.
What is the purpose of testing the mechanisms in Vegreville? Is it to provide a trap that will provide an instant kill for, say, a marten, a fisher, or a mink? What is instant? One minute, two minutes, a maximum of three minutes? That is pretty fast.
There are other traps such as the leg-hold trap. We heard the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate on the wrong track on that issue. Recently there has been some extensive testing conducted at the University of Minnesota on behalf of the Canadian Government and the Fur Institute of Canada to develop and determine the kind of pressures that there are on foxes in terms of emotional stresses and strains with the new type of leg-hold trap. Those tests have been very positive. Indeed, the tests show that any fox in a wild state has more pressures, more stresses, and different kinds of environmental strains on it which occur after the first 20 minutes in this revised, modernized, and scientifically developed leg-hold trap.
It cannot stop there. What this debate is really about is not what has happened today in Britain or is happening today in Britain; it is what is going to continue to happen and what has already gone on before, going back to the 1970s, going back to the birth, the spawning of the Brian Davies of this world and all of that ilk.
I refer to the animal rights peoples and the animal rights funds that sought millions of dollars and received millions of dollars in support of their efforts to bring a stop to the legitimate seal hunt of Newfoundland. What did they gain? They gained all kinds of gold to line their own pockets. There was not one receipt, not one financial statement, not one membership card-nothing. Ask Brian Davies. He will tell Hon. Members that it was the best thing he ever did in order to earn money. That is where that group is coming from.

June 1, 1988
Where has it gone? Where has it gone from that point? What is happening here in Canada? The European Economic Community and the European Parliament were the ones who initially torpedoed the fur seal. They are the ones who made the political decision to ban the fur seal in Europe. It was a decision that was based purely on politics and not on facts. They had the facts. They knew the facts.
However, it has gone beyond that. We now see the European Parliament busying itself with precise measurements for chicken coops. We must have a precise space for a laying hen. We must have a precise space for a broiler chicken. We must have a precise space for a pigpen, and a precise space for a cattle pen. That is where it is going.
Where else is it going? I was given a document recently, printed by an animal rights activist group, an extremist group. What did the document contain? In chapter and verse it laid out the manner in which to burglarize, terrorize, destroy vehicles, or break and enter a lab or a university. It sets out how to break and enter a zoo, or any facility. It sets out how to destroy the vehicles that may be there and how to run a car off the road. It tells one how to stretch a heavy steel cable painted black from one side of the highway to the other. What happens then? A car coming down the road strikes the cable, slides along the cable and off the road, and it is out of one's hair. That is the nature and the extreme to which these animal rights movements are headed. They are not out simply to vandalize a Dixie Lee chicken or a burger joint because they have meat or because they have chicken. Mr. Speaker, you are going to say: "You are really getting into extremes here". The fact is that those extremes are there. They are with us. That is what concerns me.
When we come back to Canada and trapping today, we see that we are making improvements in the development of humane traps. Two of the traps that have been tested at Vegreville come from my riding. I refer to the spillet trap or ymir trap and the kanya trap from the Slocan Valley. A gentleman of 70 years of age tested and tested his traps for a very long time and then developed them to the point that they could be tested at Vegreville.
I go back to the point that we are only spending $600,000 per year on the trapping fraternity of Canada, on all those indigenous people and their way of life, and that is all we are prepared to lay out. It goes further than that. It is not just trapping. It is hunting. When the animal rightists have succeeded in altering that milieu, that type of environment, then they will move on to fishing. I ask Hon. Members: "Do not think that that is some kind of idle suggestion?" It has already been espoused by the guru himself, Brian Davies.
What is needed is a plan that has been well thought out, well worked out, a plan that pays attention to the balance of our ecology.
The people who are hurt the most in all of this are the people who can least afford it. What we have are the animal rights people attacking, for example, the indigenous people,
but not necessarily. They also attack the trapper, the hunter, that element of society. Once successful they remove them. Successfully removing them for what-for industrial development, for that pipeline that might otherwise not have been approved, for that large industrial complex that might not otherwise been approved because there were several trappers there, tribes, or groups of indigenous people. We have got them out of the way because we have removed from them their lifestyle. That is what the animal right movement accomplishes or can accomplish. The philosophy of the animal rights movement can then unconsciously serve the interests of the developer rather than the indigenous peoples of this country.
It is the British who have the fox and the hounds. It is the hounds that tear apart the fox. They tear it to shreds after they have chased it to death. That society condones that. At the same time it seeks to impose its will upon us while it subscribes money to hedgehog hospitals. What a mockery.
It is the reality of today that we provide a system of understanding. We should be prepared to invest substantially in the education of Canadians and also of people of other nations about what Canada is all about-that huge land of mystery with only 26 million people who must live off the land and have lived off the land since the day that the indigenous peoples arrived along the Arctic shores.
Today, at the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development, I had the privilege to move that 5,000 copies of that committee's excellent publication in 1984 be published. On reconsideration, that was increased to 10,000. The committee has approved that. Earlier today, in response to a question that I put, the Minister indicated his support of that publication, with the view in mind of the European press, the world press at the Economic Summit, having an opportunity to receive a copy of that excellent publication. It is the creature of a great deal of work by the Standing Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and all its members in 1984.1 am proud to have played a small role in that regard. In March, I was also pleased to have the opportunity to discuss those concerns on animal rights and where the fur trade was heading with colleagues in the United States-a couple of Senators and a couple of Congressmen-with a view to developing an over-all plan required to offset the negative, damaging, and deceitful impact of the animal rights movement.
Therefore, I urge the House to consider the development of a long-range plan in terms of the explanation, the understanding, and the acceptance of trapping. In that context, we must start in the schools. In the same context, we must move to a better understanding of hunting, the balance of nature, and how that works.
It is interesting to note that the provincial Ministers have shown an interest and concern in coming together to determine what they as Ministers of the Environment or Ministers
June 1, 1988

responsible for wildlife may do to assist Canada in the development of a master plan. It will take a great deal of work and money. There is nothing very sexy about someone in a white fur coat being shot on the street and thrown over a pack horse to demonstrate that this is what happens to the animal. It has a great deal of shock and audience appeal in the context of shock.
We must take a lesson from such people as Allan Herscovici and Second Nature, a very excellent text. The public would be well served to take the opportunity to read some of the statements that he has provided.
I would like to conclude with a brief remark made by Mr. Herscovici who said: "The root of our ecological crisis lies in technology, urbanism, and wealth. Animal rights groups, however, have to date attacked those who live closest to the land, who are poorest, and who have remained relatively aloof from mass technological society". Let us come up with a master plan.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that we can have order in this debate. It is a very serious debate. We are not only attempting to address Canadians or our colleagues in the House, but we are seeking to get a message to Britain. We hope that Members of the British Parliament will have an opportunity to read these Debates, or we could send them a video tape in order that they could receive the message from all of Canada on our concerns in terms of the motion before their House.
I wish to begin by reading from a letter with the letterhead of "10 Downing Street". The person who signed the letter is the Prime Minister, Margaret Thatcher. She indicates in the letter that this matter "is still the subject of consultation". While she understands that we have concerns in this country, she states that "we must also take account of the widespread public concern here in the U.K. about the use of leg-hold traps. There is strong pressure for a ban on the import of furs ... ", and the letter continues.
The proposition that I wish to put before this House is that the action that Britain is considering is presently at the stage of study and consultation. Prime Minister Thatcher refers to that and refers to coming to a final decision. The counsel that I would like to give to the British Prime Minister is for more study and consultation. She ought to reflect upon this matter in full before coming to a decision. She ought not to make a decision on this matter on the basis of widespread public concern or strong pressure. She ought to be looking at the merits of the case. While she says in the letter "there is strong pressure for a ban on the import of furs", and that the United Kingdom is being pushed to have a ban, she later states that the U.K. is being nice because it will label the products instead, and that this is a minimal response.
We do not want to be fobbed off with a minimal response, which leaves us with a sense of guilt that we are doing something wrong and the British Parliament is being nice to
us. We would like them to take the time to study this issue and come to a moral conclusion. In other words, if furs from trapping ought to be banned and a solid and sound argument can be made for that, that is the irrefutable conclusion, then ban them; however, consider the matter first and fully and make the decision on the basis of merit, not of public pressure.
Surely if there is one Leader on this globe who has demonstrated a capacity to make decisions on the basis of principle, it is the Prime Minister of Great Britain. I fundamentally disagree with many of her principles, but I call upon her to provide leadership and to make a decision in this regard on the basis of principle. She should continue with the study and consultation and reflect some more on the issue take the time to come to a full and reasoned conclusion, and not just respond to public pressure.
What we as parliamentarians are faced with is a battle for the public mind. That is evident from Margaret Thatcher's letter in which she says that they must take into account widespread public concern. We have to win over the public if we are to win over the British Government and preserve the trapping industry in this country.
I think the fundamental question here is one of balance. On one hand we have animals and on the other we have people. The animal rights movement has done a very effective job of putting forward the case for protecting animals. I have nothing against them for doing that. However, there is another story which has to influence the decision if it is to be just and moral. The other side of the balance is people and communities. What happens to them if the industry is destroyed? I believe their case could be imaginatively and graphically presented if we took it upon ourselves to do so.
A hundred years or so ago there lived a great British writer, Jonathan Swift. The children of Ireland were starving and he used his pen to get that point across. The way he did it was to say: "We have so many children here that we ought to market them. We ought to chop them up like beef and sell them". He drew such a horrid picture that people became fully aware of the suffering of those children. We need to do the same thing today with respect to trappers. We have to do it through television, of course, because that is the way we communicate. We use television images. We have to be able to tell the British people that if they destroy the trapping industry, if they destroy the livelihood'of aboriginal communities in the North, they will have increased unemployment, increased alcoholism, and increased suicide. To achieve a real balance, for every bleeding animal they see on television they should also see the dead bodies of those who have committed suicide as a result of the destruction of this industry.
If the people of Britain want to make a moral decision they have to have a balance. They have to consider the people and their communities. Those communities include more than northern communities. In the City of Winnipeg where I come

June 1, 1988
from and in which my riding is located we have many people involved in the fur industry. It is not just a northern question.
Another aspect of this question is this: Where is the good in the issue of trapping and harvesting? I suggest that when it comes to using natural resources, the difference between use and abuse of a resource is again a question of balance. You have to balance your use against your need. If you look at aboriginal practices, history, and culture, it is easy to learn. Aboriginal people have historically taken from the land what was needed for sustenance; they have not done what we do today, rape the land and destroy the environment. If you take what you need from this planet, I suggest that what you are doing is good. That is not only true with respect to historic and traditional native values. It is also true in the western Christian tradition. The Bible says that we should take dominion over all of this. You name the animal. That is the theological, moral and spiritual basis for describing the taking of something for your own use and sustenance as good rather than evil.
There is another sense in which the question we are faced with today is one of balance. I want to speak about this historically and then in modern terms. Historically there is a question of balance between peoples. I think the Europeans are on the verge of repeating an historical mistake and once again doing an injustice to aboriginal peoples. It was the European demand for furs that created the fur industry in the first place. It was the European markets that disrupted the subsistence economy of North America. It was that market that made aboriginal peoples dependent upon European peoples. That led to undercutting the culture and way of life and spiritual values, which led to the destruction of the aboriginal way of life. That was started by the interaction among European peoples, markets, and aboriginal communities.
It was the tastes of Europe that led to the destruction of the aboriginal way of life. I am sure Europeans would not want to repeat that process because their tastes have changed and because someone thought that television advertising, through the effective use of propaganda, could sell the notion that it is wrong to wear fur, to trap and harvest animals. I ask Europeans to consider carefully their own history and to ask themselves whether they want to repeat the errors of the past.
The question of balance occurs in another way. As the Europeans look at the aboriginal peoples there are a couple of pictures to see-the pictures of trapping and of the animal suffering. People could conclude that that activity must stop because it is wrong for animals to suffer. I have already dealt with that question. I have dealt with the need to look at the other side of the coin, that is, what happens to the people. However, Europeans should look at the over-all behaviour of aboriginal peoples as they affect the environment, which is important to learn and observe. The aboriginal peoples have lived on this continent for a millennium and have preserved the environment. They have lived on this planet in harmony with the environment. Europeans should learn the values that
underlie the aboriginal way of life because we have need of those values today.
Let me turn to another point. What are we doing about preserving the Brazilian rain forests? How man McDonald's restaurants are there in Britain, and how many of those are labelled? We know that the Brazilian rain forests are destroyed to make way for massive ranches to raise cattle and have cheap beef that shows up in a fast food restaurants in the middle of London, England. That destruction alters our climate. The Europeans ought to focus on the relation between the aboriginal peoples and the environment. They should be asking questions. They should focus upon the important and big issues rather than look at things in a narrow context, forgetting that there are two sides to everything.
It is time to consider this issue and to study it in more depth. No one should rush into a decision responding to pressure campaigns that can be mounted by the electronic media.
Margaret Thatcher says that by labelling she is offering a kind of minimal response. But you can have labels and you can have labels, Mr. Speaker. The suggested label is to state that fur comes from animals that may have been caught by leg-hold traps, which is meant to project a negative image that what was done is bad. She says that the purpose is to provide information. Maybe the label ought to say that these animals have been harvested by trapping.
There are many kinds of labels and many ways to present information. Time should be taken to study the issue, to consult and reflect. Rather than responding to pressure, one should consider that by coming to a just decision one not only considers what happens to animals but what happens to people. One has to consider what happens in a remote northern community dependent upon fishing and trapping. What happens to that community if it no longer has the revenue from trapping? What happens to a community that already may have 60 per cent to 80 per cent unemployment and is deprived of its source of income? What happens to people who have no hope in their lives? One must consider not just animals but people as well, and take time to come to a reasoned conclusion as to what may or may not need to be done.
I hope Members of the British Parliament have an opportunity to see the record of this debate and that Great Britain's Prime Minister can take the time to consider her decision. If her objective is to provide people with information, she ought to consider what kind of labelling she is getting into. First, she needs to consider the over-all question of justice and morality and the whole question of trapping and making a living.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this important debate this evening. The Parliament of Great Britain is referred to as the mother of Parliament by Canadians. We hope it will recognize the importance that Members of this House, representing three political Parties, place on this issue. We asked our Speaker to recognize the
June 1, 1988

June 1, 1988
by the people of the Northwest Territories. I am proud to carry it. It would be something that I would carry to Great Britain, and I would like to say that though that may be found objectionable, it would not be objectionable to me and it is not objectionable to other Canadians.
There are ways that southern-based animal activists could attempt to understand the harsh realities of life in the North, and they are unrealistic to believe that these people who rely on this industry could survive without the animals they use to trap for income.
The destruction of the Canadian fur industry would pose a much more lethal threat to healthy wildlife populations in Canada than would disease, mismanagement and starvation combined. Anyone who believes that this action will protect the wildlife of Canada does not understand what can happen through over-population.
In thousands of years the native people of Canada have trapped fur-bearing animals and they have never-and I repeat, never-endangered a single species. It is because the trappers, more than anyone else, realize that their responsibility rests with the greater good of the total environment, with the health and survival of the species, not of an individual animal. Conservation is truly a way of life for trappers. The existence of their trap lines ensures that the natural habitat will remain undisturbed and will continue to support the thousands of animals that depend upon that habitat for their survival.
It is not something that is done haphazardly. It is a controlled harvesting of a resource, just as I, as a farmer, control the harvesting of the resource on which I base my livelihood, that of the land and the soil. Trapping is regulated in Canada by provincial and territorial Governments through licences, quotas, seasons, and export permits. The Government of Canada holds that trapping is environmentally sound. It is in harmony with nature and is an important part of a cultural life in this country.
It is not only Members in this House of Commons representing three political Parties who recognize that. In World Conservation Strategy, the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources states:
Conservation is ... the management of human use of the biosphere so that it may yield the greatest sustainable benefit to present generations while maintaining its potential to meet the needs and aspirations of future generations. Thus conservation is positive, embracing preservation, maintenance, sustainable utilization, restoration and enhancement of the natural environment.
Canadians have much to be proud of in this context. There are 20 major fur-bearing species trapped in Canada. After several centuries of trapping, none of these species is endangered. Good trapping practices have resulted in good wildlife conservation.
In fact, the people of Great Britain should know, stemming from beaver hats, that the beaver has been a heavily trapped species in this country. It may now be more populous than it has ever been before. To maintain the validity of their licences, in some provinces, Ontario for example, trappers must trap a minimum percentage of beaver as part of their annual quota. That is required because if that resource were left unharvested it would destroy itself.
The Constitution of Canada recognizes and affirms the unique rights and special status of Indian, Inuit, and Metis people within the Canadian Confederation. These rights are being debated and have yet to be fully defined in law, but trapping is clearly regarded by the aboriginal peoples of Canada as a fundamental right. I do not find that strange. The Government of Canada has a responsibility to protect the right of aboriginal people to determine their way of life. Trapping is integral to their land claims and their spirituality and culture. Without trapping there would be a great loss of self-identity and self-worth.
Trapping and hunting have allowed aboriginal peoples to walk the fine line between their traditional lifestyle and assimilation into the industrial world. That has been their choice and that, of course, is a choice that they should be allowed to make.
In conclusion I would like to read into the record, not my words, not the words of someone from south of 60, not the words of someone unfamiliar with the needs of people in northern Canada, but the words of Stephen Kakfwi, the President of the Dene nation. He spoke to the Arctic Institute of North America in the winter of 1985. As we all know, Mr. Kakfwi is now a Minister of the Government of the Northwest Territories, duly elected by the people of his constituency. Mr. Kakfwi said:
My people have cherished and protected our land for centuries and will continue to do so in the future.
To a people who continue to live in close contact with the natural world, and who have always viewed ourselves as part of that world, the argument that trapping is cruel just doesn't ring true.
We know that there is no humane death in nature. Animals that die of disease, or starvation, or fall prey to predators, suffer.
On the other hand, we are appalled at many of the cruelties that industrial society imposes on animal populations. For us, the thought of an animal living its life pent up in a cage, with its only purpose being to await slaughter for someone's table-that is cruelty.
We understand that many people are worried about the loss of wildlife species throughout the world. We share this concern.
But we also know that the greatest threat to animals is not from hunting and trapping. It is from the destruction of their natural habitat by the industrial society-by pollution and encroachment on natural areas that provide shelter to animal populations.
He concluded:
We believe we can offer our knowledge and experience as a people who live in close contact with nature to help change this dangerous trend.
I really hope that the Members of the House of Commons and the House of Lords in Great Britain, the people of Great
June 1, 1988

Britain, and the people of Canada recognize the importance of this emergency debate on an issue supported by all three Parties in this Chamber; indeed, supported by thousands of Canadians who are represented in this Chamber. I would suggest that those Canadians would support the trappers and aboriginal people in Canada. If it comes to making decisions to retaliate against something that can be done without cost by another country imposing something on an industry and a people who are very important, it must receive the support of this Chamber and the people of Canada.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to join in the debate this evening resulting from the motion before us. The Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) and the Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall) called for an emergency debate with regard to considerations being made by the British Government to apply labelling to fur goods on sale in British shops which could lead to a large-scale boycott of the fur products.
1 am pleased to join in the debate, not because it is a happy matter. Quite the contrary, it is a matter of enormous importance to many Canadians. It is a matter of enormous importance to people across the North and in that context it is very appropriate that my friend, the Hon. Member for Yukon, should have requested the debate. It is also a matter of enormous concern across northern Ontario, which makes it so very appropriate that the Hon. Member for Timiskaming should have put the motion forward.
In my area of northwestern Ontario, specifically in the constituency of Thunder Bay-Nipigon, a great deal of fur trapping is carried on as part of the livelihood of aboriginal people and residents of various communities including the City of Thunder Bay.
In these circumstances it is of enormous importance to consider what would be the impact of this British proposal. Not wanting in any way to get into a competition, because I recognize the involvement of a government private Member and my colleague in asking for this debate, I think it might be of interest to all of us in the House and to those listening across the country to be aware of how longstanding the concern about the threat to fur trapping in Canada has been.
As long ago as 1985 the federal council of the New Democratic Party dealt with the situation in a way which focused on the importance of fur trapping and the necessity for the real, strong action which we have been seeking evidence of from the government in Question Period today and at other earlier times. Our resolution declared:
Whereas the fur industry in Canada is worth $600 million to our economy; and employs 100,000 Canadians 60 per cent of whom are native; and
Whereas most native and many non-native trappers rely on trapping for a large part of their annual income; and
Whereas for native people, the harvesting of fur-bearing animals is a traditional occupation and an integral part of their way of life; and
Whereas evidence on October 15, 1985 to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development indicated that an international campaign to destroy the livelihood of Canadian trappers is well underway; and
Whereas the success of such a campaign would result in catastrophic loss of income and social disruption such as that already caused by the European ban on seal pelts,
Therefore be it resolved that the New Democratic Party of Canada calls for:
(1)	Support for trappers and recognition of the importance of trapping to the economy and society of northern, native and rural parts of the country;
(2)	Immediate and substantial funding for the development and presentation of the Canadian trappers' side of the story to Canadians and to the public of those countries where inaccurate and unfair representations of the industry are being made;
(3)	Scientific baseline studies on the populations of all fur-bearing animals in Canada;
(4)	Evaluation of all available technologies on trapping methods.
Be it further resolved that the NDP calls on the Government of Canada and on our fellow parties in the Socialist International to protect and enhance the livelihood of trappers, particularly native Canadians.
In that resolution was a clear statement by the New Democratic Party of the importance of trapping as a basis for the livelihood of 100,000 Canadians, 60 per cent of whom are natives. Trapping was a vital source of income for these people and an essential part of their lifestyle.
The place of trapping in the life and livelihood of aboriginal people of Canada deserves particular recognition. There are some profound ironies in this regard, because across the vast reaches of this country where trapping is so important, who was it that made trapping a fundamental activity in the lives of these people? Surely it was the British subjects in early days, particularly those in the Hudson's Bay Company, who saw to it that this was how people would live.
Life before that was one of subsistence, in which hunting and fishing were important and furs would only be obtained for use as clothing and shelter, not for the purpose of sale. It was the fur trade from Europe, particularly Britain and the markets in London, that changed the lives of the aboriginal peoples in the North.
The extent of this transformation is well worth considering. Before the fur trade aboriginal peoples were more closely tied to the land, perhaps only moving from a summer fishing area to a winter hunting area. It was an almost symbiotic relationship with the land on which the aboriginal peoples lived. That close relationship still exists in their understanding of themselves and the recognition of the territories in which they live even though they have been pushed back into small reserves.
The arrival of the fur trade drew them from those hunting and fishing activities into trapping of furs for sale to the traders and the ultimate use of those furs far from where they lived. Of course, this had far-reaching consequences which have been documented by historians like Harold Innis, author of a great works in the 1930s dealing with the fur trade in Canada.
June 1, 1988

One can think of more recent historians and anthropologists who explored what the fur trade represented for native peoples of Canada. They became involved in transportation activities by relocating to live at James Bay or Hudson's Bay in order to trade with the agents and factors of the Hudson Bay Company. They may have become involved in hunting activities for these fur traders.
In all of these activities, the lives of the aboriginal peoples were transformed. They were forced into a new mould of life and were dependent on the products they obtained from trading the furs they hunted. They became dependent on the use of guns and the ammunition that had to be purchased, as well as other goods they required.
This was the impact of the British and European demand for furs. There was an incredible transformation of their lives, for good or ill, from the kind of subsistence in which they lived.
What will happen if the British proposal is adopted and the labelling goes into effect? The fur market could collapse under this impact. What will happen if the European Economic Community decides to take similar action?
After 300 years of encouragement to move into the cash market for furs, aboriginal people have become largely dependent on that livelihood. Suddenly, as a result of British government action, they are faced with the return to subsistence and worse, in which their ancestors lived centuries ago. It is not an easy transformation.
When the buffalo were virtually wiped out in the past century, the Plains native people went through a century of readjustment to a different livelihood. Such readjustment, if possible, is an enormously costly and drawn out process. There must be an alternative.
What is the alternative in this case if the British succeed in destroying the trade and remove from the hands of our aboriginal people the source of livelihood and self-respect that has come to form the basis on which they relate to the land and resources around them? What process of readjustment will result from that? Those who speak of this action as being an act of "cultural genocide" do not exaggerate. We can only expect the most catastrophic of consequences.
These steps are being taken in a country which columnist Jeffrey Simpson recognized in an article last February in The Globe and Mail was characterized by the most profound of contradictions. He said very nicely in his column on February 20:
Six years ago, when the Irish Republican Army detonated a bomb that killed men and horses in London's Hyde Park, public sympathy for the horses rivaled that for the men.
He went on:
The British, you see, have this thing about animals. They chase foxes across the countryside, blast away at pheasant and grouse and run horses ragged over steeplechase courses. They race pigeons, train frogs to jump and, like the rest of us, slaughter livestock.
He went on:
The British chase, kill, maim and revere animals. They also like to set
standards for how others should treat animals, which partly explains why the
British Government will now require certain fur products to carry a label
indicating that the fur came from animals caught in leg-hold traps.
That final observation of his is the one we want to stop.
Members of the House, representatives of all three Parties as the Minister of Northern Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) recognized a moment ago, stand united on this issue. Canadians have had to stare hard at this issue, this question of the extent to which we will be obsessed with the rights of animals. None of us wishes cruelty to animals. We have as much of the sense that is involved in the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals among us as I am sure there is among all the fine people in Great Britain who are pushing this. We want to see research done on more humane methods of trapping.
We urge the British Government to join in that effort to provide funding and to advance the cause. But we are not ready in any of our Parties in this Parliament to sacrifice people to the sentiment about animals. We are simply not prepared to see the lives of people changed, transformed, as I have already indicated, from fur trade for over 300 years of activity, by this sudden obsession, which people in Great Britain have in one particular area, to focus on these furs, ignoring completely all of those who are still enjoying meals of meat and in other ways benefiting from the uses we make of animals. We are simply not prepared to see a blow at people in our country. As somebody has said, that may be done at seemingly no cost to the British people.
I was interested to hear the Minister of Indian Affairs suggest ways in which British enterprise might experience a Canadian reaction. I was interested to hear him indicate some of the well-known British enterprises operating in Canada which might find themselves experiencing boycotts organized by those who support the aboriginal peoples in their desire to go on trapping, to go on maintaining their livelihood as they have for so long.
That is an important statement of determination. We see even more from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) that we want to have real evidence that the Government is pressing the British Government and Parliament to give it up. We want to see real evidence that the British people are aware of the concern of Canadians.
Recognizing that the Press Gallery is not exactly proud of this evening, I ask myself whether the British people, through the BBC, might be made aware of what we are debating. It is of course night hours over there, but tomorrow's news should give at least a short focus on this debate in the Canadian Parliament which is expressing concern about what the mother of Parliaments intends to do to people whose lives it has affected so profoundly in centuries past and now should not be considering destroying.
June 1, 1988

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I never thought I would see the day when I would stand in this Parliament and speak to the mother of Parliaments. However, I am very pleased and proud to have this opportunity to participate in this emergency debate.
I congratulate you, Sir, the Speaker, for allowing this debate to happen. I congratulate all Members from all three Parties of the House who have participated in this debate. We are seeing a totally non-partisan debate. This is Parliament at its best, when it speaks with one voice on behalf of all the people of our great country.
You, Sir, may wonder why I as an urban Member, a Member from the nation's capital, representing a constituency in Ottawa, speaking to a debate that relates to the importance of our fur industry. I want to speak because my background is as a wildlife biologist. 1 studied biology and majored in wildlife management at the University of Ottawa. I have worked in this profession in Africa, Central America, and with Parks Canada. I want to speak because I think it is important. We are talking about an essential way of life for tens of thousands of Canadians in all our 10 provinces and both our territories.
I am also speaking because I love our renewable wildlife resources, as do the people who hunt and trap them. This is their farm. This is their life. This is their livelihood. No one should take it away from them.
If you think, Mr. Speaker, that no one traps around the National Capital Region, around Metro-Ottawa, you are wrong. Just 28 miles west of this city there is the little town of Dunrobin. In that town there is a man named Harvey Boucher. He traps for beaver and muskrat in the spring and in the wintertime. There is a man who works for the Sunday Herald, one of our newspapers, whose name is Ken Lehman. He traps beavers on behalf of the National Capital Commission. He relocates them to areas where they will not be doing damage to vegetation or flooding of people's backyards-in this city, the capital of Canada. That is something I want to get across to Great Britain.

I have another friend who lives in the Ottawa area, north of our capital, and his name is Aurele Knight. In winter, my friend Mr. Knight traps beaver. He also traps other animals. That is his life and he is very, very proud of it.

It is people like him who make this our way of life. This is Canada. This is, as some people call it, the great white North. Our country was explored, built and developed by people from the Hudson's Bay Company and other pioneering people who explored our northern regions.
Since I have been a Member of Parliament I have had an opportunity to visit other regions of our country. I want to review some of the great places I have seen in Canada. While I am doing this, I invite all British parliamentarians to take out an atlas of Canada and to review the size of this country. Let
me speak to them and say that all of Great Britain, all of it, can be put-now get your atlas-inside Hudson Bay five times. That is the size of this country that we are speaking of. I want the House of Lords and the House of Commons to understand that. Lake Superior-stay near your atlases-is .6 times the size of all of Great Britain. That is what I want to talk about.
Keep your atlas because we are going to go to a place called Old Crow in the Yukon. Go to the Yukon. Find the Yukon. See how big it is. 1 visited Old Crow with the Hon. David Crombie, the former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and former Secretary of State. I was struck by one of the villagers I met there. There are only about 300 people living in Old Crow.
I had a discussion with Norma Cassie who is one of the leaders of the community. I said: "Norma, what do you do here in the spring and summer?" She said: "We go rattin' because you sure as hell can't grow tomatoes and lettuce in permafrost".
Stay in your atlas. We are going to go on to Eskimo Point which is on the west side of Hudson Bay. I had the pleasure of hunting with the Member of Parliament for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Suluk). His people hunt caribou and seal and they trap and hunt foxes. I thought that I was so smart and knew something about the outdoors. I will never forget that I had a pair of boots made in southern Canada which I thought were warm. We were going hunting on his skidoo and it was minus 30 degrees. He said: "You can't leave until you get better boots". I said: "These are good boots. Look at the felt lining". He said: "You won't last 20 minutes on the skidoo. The chill factor is minus 50". He went through his village, and what did he find for me? I am fairly tall and I needed big boots. The people in the North are not very tall. He found a pair of caribou skins that I wore. They kept my feet warm. The villagers said: "You can't wear felt boots with rubber outside because you will not survive in this part of the world. You need skins from caribou, and that is what I wore.
Stay in your atlas, House of Lords, we are going to Tuk-toyaktuk near the Beaufort Sea. We have travelled 2,000 miles across the North. In Tuktoyaktuk I ate caribou. When I asked the people: "What do you do with the caribou?" They said: "We eat it, Sir. We use the skins for clothing and boots." I asked: "What do you do with the horns?" They said: "We carve them and sell them to the southerners, because that is our way of life in the North."
Let us go to Manitoba, a place called Reed Lake. I was there four days ago. It is in northwest central Manitoba. I spent some time with a trapper and a fisherman named Corky Peterson, and his son Hal. I was also in the presence of Bob Carmichael, who is the chief of commercial wildlife management for the Manitoba Wildlife Department. He is a real pro. He works in renewable resources. That area is not over-

June 1, 1988
trapped. It is well managed and conserved. The trapping of beaver, marten, fox and muskrat by Corky and his son is a well-managed wild-life activity. They are not at all endangered. It is in his best interest to maintain the resource to the best of his ability.
In Reed Lake I also met a man named Paul Vincent. He has 850 acres outside of the City of Winnipeg, one of Canada's largest western cities. He has a muskrat farm where dozens of people work. His business and industry are being threatened by the possible introduction of this initiative by Great Britain.
The animal rights people, the "antis" as they are called, have it all wrong. On March 10 I moved a motion in the House that asked the Government to do everything it can to enhance our wildlife resources. I have spoken on this issue all over Canada in the last three years. As one might say, I have been busting my buttocks to see that the Government spends more to manage this resource more effectively. With the help of the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), and his colleagues in Cabinet, some day we will have more moneys allocated to enhance our wildlife resources.
The animal rights people and the "antis" have it all wrong. Most of them live in a cloistered, urban, downtown environment. Let us return to the atlas and remember what we are talking about. Great Britain can fit five times inside Hudson Bay. That is the dimension that I wish to remind the British House of Lords and House of Commons that we are dealing with. I invite them all to get out into the real resource world and see what they have been missing. Come to Canada and visit this country. Experience its vastness, its diversity, and its dependence on the natural resources, particularly our people in the North.
It has been said that some of them care more about wildlife than they do about people. Our wildlife is directly related to our people. Our people are directly related to our wildlife. They depend on it. They protect it. They manage it. Yes, they harvest it, but this is their way of life in a great part of our country. Therefore, they should be allowed to trap, whether they are sealers or hunters. This is an important historical part of the building of our country.
It is in their personal and professional interest to do so and to perpetuate this resource through respecting quotas and good management practices set by the world's best wildlife biologists. Professional Canadian wildlife biologists are world famous. They work for the Canadian International Development Agency in countries all over the world. They work for the Canadian Universities Services Overseas all over the world. They work for non-governmental organizations all over the world because they are the best and are highly respected in professional fields. The Canadian non-governmental organization community, such as the Canadian Wildlife Federation, Wildlife Habitat Canada, Ducks Unlimited, the Ontario Federation of Anglers and Hunters, and hundreds of fish and game clubs are all involved in the process of protecting and enhancing the wildlife resources of this country.
How many people have ever visited an abattoir? How many people really know how domestic animals die, for example, chicken, pigs, cows, sheep? I dare say it is not too pleasant in some circumstances. How do fish die? Most of us eat fish. How do they die when they are caught in the nets at sea? They suffocate. I dare say Members of the House of Lords and the House of Commons in Great Britain eat fish. Nobody is up in arms saying: "Kill the fish humanely, or don't kill them at all". Let us remind ourselves of some of these facts. We all eat for our survival.
Our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) spoke tonight in the debate. He made reference to the international humane trapping standards committee. As an appropriate mechanism to address this problem, Canada has suggested that Great Britain become a member. I invite Great Britain to consider seriously this timely and appropriate proposal from our Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Let me send this message to the people and all elected MPs of Great Britain. We have a saying in this country: "You use it or you lose it". If we do not use our renewable wildlife resources to the best of our collective ability, we will all lose it.
The Queen's Footguards in London have that great tradition of red tunics and black hats. The black hats are made from what? Bear skin. Canadian bear skin. I ask the House of Lords if it wants to see the uniforms of decades of tradition replaced with some North Sea synthetic: "Do you want to see that happen?" I do not believe you do, because you are a people of true, long-lasting, and important traditions. Therefore, maintain the Queen's Footguards as they have been for decades, and maintain that important link with our country through the hats that they wear, that we also have here on Parliament Hill. We are proud of that. The people of the world come to this nation's capital to see the changing of the guard, which is a true, British tradition with Canadian black bear fur hats.
I say to the people in Great Britain and their parliamentarians, please reconsider your proposed actions regarding furs. Do not let your emotions overcome your reason. Our people depend on it.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) used a phrase which I believe all the world should be aware of, that extremists may care more for animals than they care for people. I would like to carry that one step further. The extremists may have a detrimental effect on wildlife as well as on people. The absurdities of the ban on seal hunting, for example, may not be known for another generation. Yet when they are, we are going to find the seal population has more than doubled. That means that seals will be eating an additional one million tonnes of the cheapest and healthiest protein supply available to people around the world. In addition, nature's way of thinning a population, which is usually disease,
June 1, 1988

will probably have a detrimental effect on a wider part of our wildlife than just the seal itself.
I think the record of this country and its environmental laws are probably the best of any in the world. We have denied ourselves great economic advantage from British Columbia to New Brunswick in order to preserve the ecological and animal life of our country. We have denied ourselves the opportunity to use a renewable resource, water, for the generation of energy, the cost of which has gone up four or fivefold in the last 15 years. It could have gone down if we used all of our water resources without considering the environment.
What then is expected of Canada? Should we not have developed James Bay? When it was developed, billions of dollars were given to the native people affected to sustain them and compensate them for the loss of their environment. What more can we be expected to do? We have banned the seal hunt, not only of grey seals but of all seals. As a result, we now have harbour seals all over the east coast of North America and the islands off that coast, and the result has been millions of dollars of damage to fishing gear and the loss of hundreds of thousands of tonnes of fish devoured by those seals.
We have possibly created a situation in the sea, in response to the extremists, comparable to that of the rabbits and the fox on land. When the fox population drops, the rabbit population multiplies. I predict that somewhere down the road we will see a similar situation with the seal because of the ban on hunting. The seals will either die of disease en masse or starve to death because they have depleted the fish stock. This is a self-defeating exercise by the European Economic Community. It wants greater opportunities to fish in the Canadian waters of the North Atlantic, yet it will have less and less opportunity as the seal population multiplies.
If we go to the Pacific coast we find that Senator Stevens of Alaska is now saying to the U.S. Government that it has to remove the ban on the seal hunt and the whale hunt. Whales have now reached a population level such that they are appearing in waters in which they had never appeared before. They are preying upon the salmon stock, among others, on the west coast of North America. Senator Stevens, who is nothing if not interested in the environment, fishing, the caribou and all those other things that sustain his native population, is complaining to his Government that it has to do something about the seals and the whales. They are destroying fishing gear and eating fish to a degree that is very detrimental to the fishing community.
How, then, can we respond to the extremist who does not recognize the negative effect on wildlife caused by overpopulation? I believe it is a kindness to control that population.
In New Brunswick the coyote was on the protected list. Do not hunt it, do not kill it, do not trap it because it has not existed in any numbers at all for generations. What is the situation now? The deer and moose populations are suffering depredation. Domesticated animals are being attacked in their pastures or barns because the coyote population is far in excess
of the natural supply of food available to them. We have protected the coyote beyond a rational point and we may just have to put a bounty on it to protect both wildlife and domesticated animal life in the Province of New Brunswick.
I am of course concerned about the dollars that accrue to trappers, native or otherwise. However, I do not think the dollar is all that counts. It is also important to recognize that it is a kindness to wildlife to keep their numbers under control so that they are comfortable in their environment and healthy. I do not believe it is right to go the route proposed in the United Kingdom or the route followed in the European Economic Community with respect to the seals.
It seems rather strange that on the one hand the UN is happy to listen to the aboriginal people of the world, whether they be from Greenland, Canada or Australia, but on the other hand, because it is listening to the extremists in the wildlife groups, those people are being starved because they are not being allowed to hunt a resource in a way which would not threaten it but would control its numbers. It is ironic that the aboriginals of the world can get sympathy in the UN while at the same time being denied this economic opportunity.
It is not that members of the EEC do not know what has happened. This situation has been presented to them before. At a meeting of the Canadian Parliamentary Association with the European parliamentary group there was present a gentleman from Greenland. He was pleading with us to support him because the native people of his country had lost 75 per cent of their income as a result of the ban on seal hunting. That was a pretty harsh sentence to impose upon the native people of Greenland by extremists and those who care little really for mankind which depends upon the life of this world. Mankind always has and always will be dependent for food on the vegetable and animal life of this world, whether it be ocean or land oriented. We shall always be dependent upon the animal and vegetable life of the land and sea for our food.
Why then should we restrict a group of people in a harsh and cruel manner? Why not allow these forest-oriented individuals to make a living, whether native or otherwise? We should appeal to the communities of the world, including the United Nations, to let us take a look at what is fair and right, what is in accord with the needs of mankind. Sure the people in the extreme North need furs to keep them warm and the people in other sections of the world enjoy wearing the furs which keep them warm. Maybe in some instances furs are a status symbol. Nevertheless I believe that since we are all dependent upon this form of life and the food and clothing supplied by them, we should have a rational control of populations as we did have with the seals in Canada. They should not be allowed to get out of control to the detriment of all the seal species and in the long run to the detriment of the food supply of the world.

June 1, 1988

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is ironic that the very nation which some centuries ago sent explorers to this continent and subsequently large fur companies to disturb the balance and the equilibrium that existed at that time between the aboriginal people in this land and the animals which they hunted for fur should now be attacking those people again. These are the people whose very balance with nature they destroyed in the past and now they seek to destroy again by this action proposed by the Government of Great Britain in the form of a ministerial order which would have all furs, irrespective of their source, labelled to the effect that they may have been obtained as a result of leg-hold traps.
I am a biologist, Mr. Speaker. As a biologist I respect life. But I understand the differences that exist in that vast array of entities in this world that we call life. One thing that I recognize is that animal liberation organizations apparently do not understand the difference between human life and human existence and the value of humanity as compared to animals.
It offends me greatly that there are those who would place a higher value on animals of any sort than they would upon human existence, even upon the existence of human beings that could teach those city dwellers in Great Britain what it is all about to live a life of respect for nature and in balance with nature. The aboriginal peoples of this country, whether pertaining to seals or to fox, respected those living entities. They understood that their survival depended upon their exploitation to a certain limit. They also understood that they are a part of an ecological chain in which the fox kills smaller animals in order to survive. The aboriginal peoples, up until this day in the North and at one time throughout this country, lived the same kind of existence in that ecological balance.
Today we are faced with a group who would draw equivalents between animals and human beings. They talk about animal rights rather than animal welfare. How distorted can your thinking be if you truly believe that there is a real comparison between the existence of animals and the existence of human beings. This is a sorry example of tremendous hypocrisy perhaps more hypocrisy even than an incapacity to understand the world in which these people live. The hypocrisy of the Government of Great Britain and those who would push it to take action against the aboriginal people can be dramatized by the fact that they make much more of the existence of a fox than they would of that of an aboriginal person. This is an inconsistency from a nation which is entirely incapable of reacting to the blood of children spilled in South Africa, a Government that has refused every request for action in response to South Africa and the injustices there. This is a nation that would take strong action in response first to baby seals and now to fur-bearing animals in northern Canada and elsewhere. What kind of a nation is it that would refuse to behave in a fashion that is humane to humans but is more humane to animals? What kind of Prime Minister is Mrs. Thatcher who will not react to the oppression and the death of children in South Africa or the children, the elderly and others
in Mozambique who day by day lose their arms and legs not in leg-hold traps but by mines planted by a Government, indirectly by a Government that the Thatchers of this world refuse to condemn. This seems so inconsistent that I wonder whether there really is an inconsistency here. Isn't it rather that this is a nation led by a Government that has little humanity for aboriginal peoples anywhere? After all, in South Africa we are talking about aboriginal people. So we have a Government that places rather low value on the aboriginal people, the original people of southern Africa, and low value upon the aboriginal peoples of Canada. This kind of hypocrisy cannot be tolerated by Canadians. This is a brand of hypocrisy that would condemn our native people to penury, and this loss of way of life cannot be tolerated nor can it merely be responded to by rhetoric.
There are those who have said that there ought to be strong retaliatory action by Canada in response to this proposed action of Great Britain if it carried through with it. That we should do. We should not allow a repetition of the tragedy imposed upon those in Newfoundland who depended on, as I described, and who existed in an ecological balance with the seals, the fish and the other partners in the chain of ecology. We cannot allow it to be repeated for the northern natives, the aboriginals who depend upon fur-bearing animals.
Every Member of this House should commit himself or herself to write to Members of the British Parliament immediately to point out what a disgraceful, hypocritical action is proposed by that Government. If indeed the British proceed with that action then the Canadian people, with the leadership of this Parliament, should selectively boycott British products so that the Government of Great Britain will understand that we will not allow our people to suffer because of the hypocritical stupidity of those who would value the lives of animals above the lives of human beings.
