subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to speak on the adjournment debate concerning the move by the British Government to impose a labelling device on furs from Canada, a device which would detract from their value and would discourage people in the United Kingdom from purchasing those furs which come from Canada.
It is important that this debate take place tonight. We must send a uniform message to the British Parliament indicating that we are very concerned about this move to put in place such a regulation. We know what impact it would have on the incomes of literally tens of thousands of Canadians, most of whom live in northern regions and most of whom are at the bottom of the economic scale. These people probably earn less than those living in large urban areas. I am told that there are
June 1, 1988

at least 100,000 Canadians who still earn a living from trapping fur-bearing animals.
We normally think of this as being an activity which takes place in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon, but clearly it goes far beyond that. It takes place in northern Ontario, northern Quebec and throughout many of the northern regions of Canada. In my own constituency of Algoma, there are some 12 Indian bands, and I would say that in at least half of them some level of trapping takes place.
It is an activity carried on not only by native people. Many small farmers and land owners are also involved, and there are many people whose primary occupation is trapping. This move on the part of the Government of the United Kingdom could have an extremely adverse impact on all of these groups. These groups are composed of low-income people who live in northern areas. The only cash money they receive for income is from the sale of fur-bearing animals.
I think it is important that we send a uniform message to the British Government indicating that we are very concerned about these Canadians. Often, the only source of income they have for many months of the year is their trap lines.
It seems to me that here we have a clash of societies, a clash between the urban sophisticated society of the United Kingdom and the society of northern Canada in which native peoples and others live. Trapping is an accepted way of life in this society. In my own riding, they use those kinds of traps, kanya bear traps and others, which are not considered to be in any way cruel. From the experience I have had with trappers, I do not believe that they operate in a cruel and unjust way. They are concerned with the biological movement from generation to generation.
It is clear that the proposed action with regard to the fur trade in Canada taking place in the United Kingdom and in other European countries is the same kind of action we saw with regard to the seal hunt a few years ago, which action ultimately cancelled the whole seal hunt. It was important to those of Prince Edward Island, on the shores of Quebec and in Newfoundland while the fur industry is important to those in most provinces. I am told that it generates some $600-million worth of income a year and some $350-million worth of income in exports alone.
I want to join with Hon. Members who have spoken tonight, and with Members like the Hon. Member for Renfrew- Nipissing-Pembroke (Mr. Hopkins) who put questions to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) yesterday calling on the Government to take the strongest possible action with the United Kingdom Government in sending a very strong message. We hope that the fate that befell the seal hunt will not fall upon those who earn their living in the hard and difficult world of trapping in the northern regions. I have spoken to trappers from the federal riding of Algoma and they have told me how concerned they were about the move that took place with regard to the seal hunt. We see now in the
United Kingdom a telegraphing of possible difficulties in the future.
I simply want to join with those who have spoken tonight to urge that the United Kingdom Government back down from this action, which could have a devastating impact on tens of thousands of northern citizens, many of whom have a very difficult and onerous life as trappers.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall) as well as the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mrs. McLaughlin) for arranging this evening's adjournment debate on the proposed British fur-labelling issue.
This issue is not a partisan issue, as many which are debated in this House are. For one evening, we have managed to set aside our Party bickering because we have ascertained a common enemy. When Canadians are faced with such a common threat, they tend to set aside their differences and work together for the common cause, in this case the common cause of trappers and the fur industry.
The Government is appreciative of the support given by opposition Parties to date on this issue and the support that we expect will be forthcoming in the future, because this undoubtedly will not be the last time this matter is brought up in the House. I have spoken in the House on many occasions in the past on this particular subject, and many, perhaps more eloquently than I, have spoken on the issue tonight. What I am about to say will be somewhat repetitive, but I hope to keep it fairly short.
The seriousness of the threat is not to be underestimated. It is something of the thin edge of the wedge. What starts out as a labelling requirement in one European country could spread to other European countries which constitute a large market for furs, and the labelling could, over a period of time, escalate into a total ban. It could have, in the long run, a devastating effect on our fur industry. The seriousness is demonstrated by headlines that appeared in The Globe and Mail on May 30, just a couple of days ago. One such headline reads "Fur Industry Jeopardized by Activists". On another page of the same newspaper, as the article continued, the headline reads "Activists Threatening Canada's $350 million in Fur Exports".
Therefore, interest in this issue is not restricted geographically to Canada. It is one in which all Canadians from rural, far northern, and major metropolitan areas can join together. It affects all aspects of the fur industry from the trapper or rancher to the traders, to the auction houses, to the factories, to the garment manufacturers, and the people involved in sales. Earlier this evening the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) told us that it was a $1 billion industry in Canada with about $350 million worth of exports.
I intend to restrict my remarks mainly to the northern trapper because those are the people whom I have the honour

June 1, 1988
of representing in the House. I will do so by quoting from three letters from people who are all more knowledgeable on this subject than I am myself. The first letter is from a gentleman who has already been quoted once this evening in the House of Commons. I am going to quote from a different letter from the Right Reverend John Sperry, Bishop of the Arctic. He wrote a letter to the Prime Minister of Great Britain in which he says:
As the Bishop of the Arctic, with some nearly 40 years of residence in the Northwest Territories, I have lived with and served a people, both Indian and Eskimo (Inuit) who for centuries have survived only because of their relationship to and the harvesting of the animals that inhabited their land and waters.
For these people throughout their history lifestyles have certainly undergone changes but, for centuries, always in the colonial relationship they experienced under the British Monarchy and its Governments no challenge was ever given to their deep cultural affiliation to the land. This affiliation has always and necessarily involved harvesting by both hunting and trapping, the whole industry being given dramatic input by a succession of Europeans who opened up the Canadian Northwest for both exploration and commerce.
The alleged action proposed by your Government to label Canadian fur products in such terms as to stigmatize the labour of the native trapper is viewed by many of us as little short of an act of cultural genocide upon a small minority of people who for so long have held the British Monarchy and its Governments in deep respect for their understanding of what life and survival on the most northerly frontier of the Commonwealth really entails; this threatened stance of your Government could prove to be a shattering experience for our people.
The second letter, Mr. Speaker, is from the Hon. Titus Allooloo, Minister of Renewable Resources with the Government of the Northwest Territories. It is addressed to the Right Honourable Joe Clark, Secretary of State for External Affairs, and is with regard to the proposed fur labelling legislation by the British Government. It reads:
The Government of the Northwest Territories wishes to express its strongest objections to proposed actions by the British Government to legislate a requirement of retailers to prominently display labels on products which contain the pelts of wild animals that may have been caught with a "steel-jaw leghold trap".
Once again, we experience the highest levels of frustration, and indeed indignation, that foreign governments and/or agencies are taking actions without due regard to the detrimental consequences their actions have on the basic livelihood of groups of people around the world.
I request your assistance on communicating to the British Government our total rejection of such a proposal. In addition, we would offer to, once again, present our positions to them in the most effective manner possible, including direct representation.
We have appreciated your high level of support in the past to counter these measures. The funding support to lobby organizations, such as the Fur Institute of Canada and Indigenous Survival International, are good examples of your dedicated support.
We thank you also for your prompt statements in the House of Commons and the media. Your proposed meeting with Sir Geoffrey Howe is of special interest to us as we feel it may prove to be a most effective action.
Our government is presently examining a variety of strategic options open to us and we shall continue to keep you advised of our planned actions.
Thank you for your support and you may be assured of our total cooperation in this matter.
The third letter with which I wish to illustrate my point, Mr. Speaker, is from Ms. Alice Hill, Executive Director of the
Native Women's Association of the Northwest Territories. In a letter dated March 14 of this year she says:
The Native Women's Association of the N.W.T. is fully supporting the Indigenous Survival International and the Fur Institute of Canada to ban England's Legislation to label fur garments regarding leg hold traps.
Our livelihood depends on fur trapping for food to feed the children, family and relatives. The fur hide is used to make moccasins, parkas, mukluks and mitts. It is used by the Dene (Indian) people of the North today. Every part of the carcass remains are used up. Monies made from the furs go right back into the Economy to purchase supplies and equipment necessary for trapping. Native women today sew arts and crafts decorated by fur. Fur has warmth and insulation for Northern climates.
The fur season is from December to February when the weather is extremely cold in the North ... During peak periods, the fur on the animals is very dense, therefore trapping is only done for approximately three months of the year.
To our understanding, work is under way to Find a new type of trap for the future, rather than the leg hold trap adversely opposed by the anti-fur lobbyist group. Despite this, families living off the land, still have to eat, live, and survive the climates and conditions of the Northwest Territories on an everyday basis.
Jobs are not so easily available to Northern Indian and Inuit people. Many (majority) of them do not have the education required to go into the labour market. Historically, Indian and Inuit people were sent off to convents and residential schools for a short period of their lives for schooling.
It was acceptable to send their children home with a Grade five or six education level so they may go back to trapping with their families. This colonization by the Government was an accepted practice. Consequently in the long run, we have many trappers depending on trapping with minimal education but very proficient as a trapper and would like to remain a trapper.
Should England legislate the label, it would have a pronounced effect on our culture and our way of life as it did with the Inuit and the Anti-Seal Campaign, which destroyed the livelihood of the Inuit people who now depend on Welfare and odd jobs.
Historically, England's demands for fur was what started the Fur Trades, and the long accomplished orientation of the Dene and Inuit to meet those demands were met, consequently, the majority of Natives in the long run are now trappers, which has carried on for generations upon generations.
Today, we ask the Prime Minister, Margaret Thatcher, NOT to legislate labelling fur garments which would jeopardize the lives of the Dene, Metis and Inuit people of the Northwest Territories.
The Native Women's of the N.W.T. would like to remind the Government of England to think of the poor Indian families and their children in making this decision.
I would like to comment on some of the actions of Governments to date. Both provincial and territorial Governments have been most active. They have sent delegations to England to try to argue the point. In the Territories a spontaneous movement has grown up. School children have written letters to the British Prime Minister and parliamentarians. A wide variety of people from that area, not only those who are dependent upon trapping themselves but the rest of the people who live there as well, have been very active in pursuing this matter.
With regard to the federal Government, we have been much better prepared with this issue than we were with the seal issue. Foreign officers, high commissioners, ambassadors and their staff know the position of the Government, thanks to the
June 1, 1988

early forceful statements made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. They have been in a good position to present the Canadian viewpoint. They have had the facts available to them.
There have been personal meetings between our Secretary of State for External Affairs and his counterpart with the Government of Great Britain, Sir Geoffrey Howe. We have been working in conjunction with the Canadian fur institute. We have been funding Indigenous Survival International, for example, for an exhibit they put in the Museum of Man in London not long ago. We have been doing everything possible to see that the British and Europeans are aware of the facts and of our Canadian concerns.
So far, what we have been able to accomplish in concrete terms is to delay the proceedings. It is interesting how we have been able to do this, at least in part, by bringing this matter to the attention of Denmark which has trapping interests in Greenland and also, I am told, fox farms in Jutland. Denmark is a member of the EEC and was able to lodge a formal protest by way of a note of notice. That has brought about a three-month stay of execution.
Now we must consider what courses of action might be available to us in the future if the British persist in this measure. Of course, we will carry on with the representations as to date and we will work with our allies, especially those in the EEC, like Denmark.
However, we must look at action that might be a little stronger. This matter is certainly what I would call a restraint of trade. We must look at the possibilities under the General Agreement on Tariff and Trade and perhaps take it to that body.
I well understand and compliment the Secretary of State for External Affairs on his reluctance to escalate this matter into something of a trade war. No one really wants to see that. He takes a much more constructive approach by suggesting such things as joint membership of Canada and Great Britain in the International Humane Trapping Standards Committee where we can work together to make sure that fur is produced as humanely as possible.
However, if we were to really look, I am sure we could find a variety of British goods that are produced in ways that might not bear too much scrutiny. I hope that this would not become necessary.
Of course, there is the question of nuclear submarines which they would like us to buy. If they want to sell them, they must keep on pretty good terms with potential customers.
If we chose, we could be just as bloody-minded as the British. Hopefully, however, they will be sensitive and sensible enough so that that does not need to happen.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to make a few comments and congratulate the Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) and the
Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall) for introducing this important topic.
The all-Party agreement on this issue must indicate to the Parliament in Britain that all of us believe the British Government proposal is unwise and is perhaps made more out of ignorance than understanding. All Parties oppose the British Government's proposal to compel the labelling of furs made from animals caught by the leg-hold trap.
This issue was first brought to my attention by my colleague, the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). One of his constituents is involved with the Canadian Fur Traders Association, and I know the Member has been concerned about the proposal by the British Government.
There is a fear that if this is successful, the fur industry in Canada will be ruined. This is an important matter because over 100,000 jobs are involved.
Presently, Parliament is caught up in a debate about free trade between Canada and the United States. The best estimate shows that there could be a net increase of some
120.000	jobs. Yet this British proposal could affect some
100.000	jobs.
This industry primarily affects aboriginal people, who have had great difficulty in adjusting to the western industrialized society. It is an industry in which they can earn an income while retaining a sense of pride.
The British Government, through its ignorance, is threatening this livelihood and has the potential to produce social and personal tragedies as the native communities no longer can make a decent living through trapping.
One can get into a philosophic debate about the role of animals in sustaining human life. Others have attempted to compare the cruelty of the slaughterhouse with trapping and the use of the leg-hold trap. However, I think those are moot points.
It should be pointed out that Canada is concerned about the humane treatment of animals and ensuring that they suffer the least amount of pain.
It is also important to point out that the meat of many animals that are trapped is more valuable to native communities because it sustains their diet. Therefore, while the British Government's proposal threatens the viability of the fur trade, it could harm native communities. Trapping is an important part of the native culture and the native tradition. Again, this tradition and this culture is being threatened tonight by the proposed actions of the British Government.
In concluding, and I assured you, Mr. Speaker, I would be brief in my remarks, the one point that I want to emphasize again is the importance of the fur trade to the aboriginal people. In my City of Regina I know many native people who have come from the country and the reserves because there

June 1, 1988
was nothing for them there. They end up in the city where, again, there is very little for them. There are poor-paying jobs, if they are available. Generally it is a life of hopelessness and despair. People have had great difficulty finding a meaningful role for themselves in modern industrialized society. There have not been many opportunities for them to participate as human beings in our social process.
One of the few areas that is open to them is in the fur trade. The action of the British Government threatens that. 1 think it is a dumb move on their part. I am certain they do not know and realize the consequences that this will have on human beings in Canada, people who have experienced the hardships of the western civilization, brought about in great deal by Great Britain and the fur traders sent out by Great Britain. They will now ironically inflict even more harm and suffering on the native people by the actions that they are proposing to take.
I take great pleasure in joining with my colleagues from all political Parties this evening in urging the Government of Great Britain to cease and desist.

speechtext: I would like to thank the Hon. Member for being cognizant of the clock. I would like to recognize the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Mr. Comeau) and then the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry) before we end the debate.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too will try to be brief because of the hour. First, I would like to say that I appreciate this opportunity to have my few words in this debate.
I cannot really believe that we continually have to get up in the House of Commons to defend industries that we have had here for centuries in Canada, and our way of life, from animal rights activists. First it was the sealing trade. Now it is the native people of Canada, the fur trappers and so on. Next it will probably be the fur farming industry of Canada.
Where will it stop? Where will the animal rights activists want to stop? Will it be with chicken farmers, hog farmers, cattle ranchers, with turkey farmers, or fishermen? Finally, will they go after the vegetable farmers because vegetables are living beings? We must surely realize that what is happening is deliberate. It is causing deliberate damage and disruption. This should be apparent to all.
In case some people may sympathize with what is being proposed by the animal rights activists, I would like to remind them that this will affect all Canadians, not only the native peoples of Canada who richly deserve our support but all Canadians. All Canadians should be alarmed and angered by the attack on our people and our economy. Canadians must realize the damage and destruction which is being caused to our communities. Canadians must realize the chain reaction effect which will touch us all. In case they may not know that we are being affected, I will give an example.
Let us take a fox ranch or a mink ranch, something which I am more familiar with. Let us say that ranchers in one of the communities in my riding, such as Little Brook, Weymouth or Havelock, who raise fur animals use the waste from the fishing industry, from the fish plants, thus acting as a waste disposal unit. Fish offal is used as food for the animals. It is a high protein food. The ranchers also use offal from chicken farms, as well as the eggs that have gone bad. These various waste products do not go to clutter up the environment. They are being used by the fur ranchers. These waste products might become quite damaging environmental problems. The carcass from the mink and fox ranches are then put to quite good use by being put into a rendering process, and what remains is used in various areas.
The chain reaction does not end there. Not only is fur farming important for the fishing and livestock industries, it is also important to the grain farmers who produce the feed that makes the food for the animals. Nobody would deny the problems that our wheat farmers and grain farmers have been undergoing over the past number of years. Fur ranchers support the lumber industry in the building of pens and in the furring sheds. Fur ranchers purchase wire for cages. So it affects the steel industry. The transport industry is affected since it transports feed to the ranches and the pelts to market.
How many jobs will be affected in the manufacturing of clothes from furs? Thousands. I could go on and on. We could mention the models who model the clothes. We could talk about the manufacturers of cardboard boxes, veterinarians and drug manufacturers. The list could go on and on.
If we as Canadians think that this is only affecting the aboriginal people of Canada-and it is affecting them and the way of life that they have held for thousands of years-it is affecting us as well, non-native Canadians. We should be reminded of this.
Centuries ago our ancestors came to Canada. One of the cornerstones of our economy, along with fishing and lumber, was the fur trade. This, I might add, is the oldest land based industry in Canada. Fur trapping and fur ranching is as Canadian as the beaver and the maple leaf. We have had a fur industry for centuries. We wish to continue for centuries into the future for the sake of our children and our grandchildren. We do not want a bunch of animal rights activists playing on the sentiments of people in order to raise funds for God knows what purpose. This is something of which I want to remind Margaret Thatcher. The company she is keeping nowadays leaves a lot to be desired.
I want to remind the British who have a sport which I think they should be looking into. I refer to the famous sport of fox hunt-tallyho and all that. I do not think that that is the way to go either. Let them look in their own backyard before coming to Canada.
Both the fur ranching and fur trapping industries are important to us. We want them to continue to maintain jobs
June 1, 1988

for our rural communities, for our native communities, and we want them here for a long period of time.
I would like to draw attention to how fast damage can be done to industries. In 1980 in our sealing industry we could not produce enough seal pelts. It was a completely open market at that time. We could sell as many as we wanted to sell. That was in 1980. In 1982, there was virtually no market at all. So I would like to pass that on as a closing comment.
I promised that I would be very brief. I am living up to my promise. I am leaving time to other speakers.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say, in rising to address this matter of the proposed fur labelling legislation in the United Kingdom, that I am very glad to have the opportunity to speak. I would like to start by thanking the Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. Mac-Dougall) and my colleague the Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin), for this opportunity. I would particularly like to compliment and express my gratitude, and that of my constituents, to the Hon. Member for Yukon who has been so involved in this issue, and who went to the United Kingdom at her own expense to pursue this matter and lobby Members of the British Parliament and of the House of Lords.
I would also like to pay tribute to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). The degree of concern that he has shown in this matter does him great credit. I believe that the support which he has given to the fur industry is much appreciated.
The range, not only geographically but in terms of ideology and demography, and the range of constituencies whose Members have spoken in this debate tonight should show, if anything can show, the degree to which this concern is felt within this country. I have heard Members from Prince Edward Island, our smallest province and cradle of Confederation, from the two Territories, from the other provinces of this country, from urban settings, rural settings, and vast remote settings like that of my own riding, or that of the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy), who is not present but who would also have liked to have spoken, ridings that are larger in size than the entire country of the United Kingdom where these regulations are proposed.
The Hon. Member for Southwest Nova (Mr. Comeau) spoke of fur farming. Because of my experience in my own riding I will speak only of the wild fur industry. What concerns me is the danger that we may be engaged in a dialogue with the deaf. After all, the Members of the British Parliament are presumably abed and do not have the opportunity to see this debate live as it is happening. We can only hope that their media sources are alert to the concerns of Canada, although
past experiences with visiting British journalists have largely been negative. We can only hope that the mother of Parliaments, whose members at the time gave this Parliament its very existence and endowed this Parliament with its very traditions right down to the minutia of the colours that we see before us, are indeed going to pay attention to what is said here and the depth of concern from which our statements spring.
The history of the fur trade in Canada is a history that is intimately linked from its very beginning to the history of the United Kingdom. Our oldest corporate identity is the Hudson's Bay Company founded by Royal Charter in England at the Palace of St. James on May 2, 1670. It was a company of gentlemen adventurers trading into Hudson's Bay, at the initiative of those great French explorers and entrepreneurs, Radisson and Des Groseilliers, but nevertheless it was a company formed in England which took as its motto Pro pelle cutem which has been roughly translated as "We will give our skin to get theirs", or "Seeking their hides at the possible cost of our own".
The under-appreciated or perhaps totally ignored reality is that the fur trade, while we now see it as being integral to the very traditions and culture of aboriginal people in this country, changed North America socially and economically at the time and in a very dramatic fashion so that tribes and entire nations relocated across hundreds, indeed, thousands of miles to pursue this trade, their first and most basic economic interaction with the European society that intruded into this continent.
I think that I can bring some very special perspectives to this debate. I can remember as a child of seven raising funds for the people's dispensary for sick animals, one of those organizations which was in the forefront of animal welfare in the United Kingdom, long before we heard of animal rights leagues. I can also remember, before I came to Canada, being represented by two Members of the British Parliament who, I believe, are still Members. Memory may serve me incorrectly, but since I studied at the University of Exeter where the Hon. Gwyneth Dunwoody, who has co-operated so well with my colleague and friend from the Yukon on this matter, was a Member of Parliament, it may be that she at one time represented me.
Having grown up in England, I think that I understand very well some of these springs and the psychology which leads to this type of regulation being proposed. As a columnist in The Globe and Mail so wittily pointed out: "Anthropomorphism is a very deep strain within the education and upbringing of the English". I am sure there are English children who believe, as I did, that rabbits run around in little blue vests, and hedgehogs might be dressed in the style and manner of Victorian grandmothers.
There is also the urban psychology. I will not go into too much detail of fox hunting in the United Kingdom, a barbarous relic described by the poet, Siegfried Sassoon, "as the

June 1, 1988
unspeakable in pursuit of the uneatable". After all, we must be fair and acknowledge that many of those whose opinions and views are behind this labelling regulation that is proposed are also opposed to fox hunting.
I would take up the point as to what constitutes cruelty, and others have made it very well. We eat steaks and we wear leather shoes. 1 respect those who avoid those things. But so many of us, in so many ways, use animals, and I believe it is far-fetched for anyone to suggest that there is more cruelty in the harvest of wild fur than there is in the confinement, breeding, and slaughter of domestic animals, whether it be for food or leather.
Let us remember the point raised that trappers do not use only the fur. They use carcasses for their own food as well as for the food of their dogs. Let us remember that nowadays, with the transition of the centuries, the fur trade and the fur harvest is so deeply entrenched in the psychology of the aboriginal people of this country that many of them see it, and quite correctly, as being their major link to that land with which they identify, that land and natural environment of which they see themselves as part, as a seamless continuum without the discontinuities of man and nature, the juxtaposition that we in our western way of thinking impose upon that environment.
Let us remember that the trapper is truly the conservationist, that no species has ever been driven into extinction by trapping, and particularly not by trapping undertaken by aboriginal people who are 60 per cent of the trappers in Canada, and perhaps 85 per cent of the trappers in my riding.
Those hunters and trappers, users of animals as they are, like the vast majority of all us, whether we live within an urban, rural, or remote environment, are the true conservationists; these are the true environmentalists. They were not the ones who drove into extinction the dodo or the passenger pigeon. That must be laid at the doorstep of those who came later.
I am somewhat reminded, in viewing this proposed fur labelling legislation by the Government of the United Kingdom, of the words of Neville Chamberlain in justifying appeasement: "Czechoslovakia is a far-off country of which we know nothing". It appears that these regulations are being introduced in the spirit that Canada is a far-off country of which Britain knows nothing, or indeed very little.
I believe that the misinformation and the lack of information that has been present in the public treatment of this issue in the United Kingdom reflects no credit on the Government of that country, and indeed reflects little credit on the popular views of many people in that country. It cannot be said that the mode of death of an animal, even one that is trapped in a leg-hold trap is something that is wilfully or arbitrarily cruel. Death is never, of course, an attractive reality. Elowever, to say this is more cruel, more arbitrary than the death of an animal kept for slaughter is making a judgment that reflects not values but simply cultural perceptions.
I recall the seal campaign and the way that that affected the livelihood of many of Canada's aboriginal peoples and the way it led to a verifiable increase in the social misery indicators in the aboriginal communities. They saw their livelihood disappear because of arbitrary decisions made in another country. Let us not be deceived. This labelling regulation is but part of a campaign aimed at the complete elimination of the fur industry. That will cause untold disruption to the economy of Canada, and particularly that of our poorest communities, the aboriginal communities. The final irony will be that these communities will be left in their final agony through the elimination of that trade which gave them their very existence.
I would of course like to continue on this subject for a very long time tonight but obviously will not do so out of respect, but only for yourself and those who serve us here, as well as for my colleagues who have limited their own remarks. However, let us not forget that the precedent being set will allow speculative, at best, and fundamentally dishonest at worst, propaganda labels to be attached to fur goods in the U.K. Let us ask the Government to pursue this further. Let us ask the Government to make a commitment to further increase research and development of humane trapping within Canada. Let us ask the Government to put this matter on the agenda with the United Kingdom at the Toronto summit. Let us urge Members of the British Parliament to consider and pass Early Day Motion 651 which speaks so eloquently of the disruption and deterioration of aboriginal societies in Canada should this labelling legislation go into law in the U.K.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   FUR TRAPPING INDUSTRY CAMPAIGN ON SALE OF CANADIAN FURS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was not aware of that arrangement. I was 100 miles out of Ottawa at a meeting tonight and I just got in and I wanted to speak in this debate.
I simply wanted to say that this debate is indeed not a modern occurrence. It is an historic debate in Canada over the fact that Great Britain is discouraging the sale of Canadian fur in that country and that pressure groups from the animal lobby are going after British politicians, obviously with results. Our minds must wander back to the days when the fur traders travelled up and down the Ottawa River past my riding for 150 miles. The canoes were those of the Northwest Company and the Hudson's Bay Company, British money. They came to Canada in those early pioneer days when Canada's staple crops, if we want to call them crops, were fish, fur and timber.
June 1, 1988

Grain was added later. Yet today, without proper research, without proper consideration for the economy of this country, we see a large organized pressure group in Great Britain come forward actually to attack the fur trade as it now exists in Canada. I must say that I am of British ancestry and I am very disappointed in what is taking place in Great Britain, as I think most Canadians are.
In our dealings with Britain, indeed other European countries, we have always been looked upon as a sort of good neighbour and good friend. Now we are being tossed aside. However, it is not the first time that Canada has been tossed aside by Britain and our other friends. In 1903 Great Britain and the United States came together and made an agreement, and Canada lost in the establishment of the boundary between Alaska and British Columbia.
Today, with the trapping industry in Canada going through a very difficult time with prices down one-third from what they were last year and with 100,000 or more Canadians who depend, if not entirely at least in part, on this industry for a living, I think it is time for our British friends to remember that Canada has done a tremendous amount for them over the years, to say nothing of the support we gave them and Europe through two major world wars. We can see the evidence of that as we look at the tombstones of our soldiers across Europe.
I think it is sad that we have come to this stage where animal lobbyists in Great Britain, without any research into the commerce flowing back and forth across the Atlantic, without any respect for the history or traditions of our two countries, are attacking this industry.
I heard one Hon. Member speaking just a little while ago about the fur hats of the Grenadier Guards in Great Britain. They forget where those hats came from. These groups are throwing that tradition aside, and it is ironic because if any country in the world loves tradition, it is Great Britain.
I would simply appeal tonight to the British Parliament, to Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and her cabinet colleagues,
to listen to these comments from the Canadian Parliament. Let them give a second thought to the situation and remember some of the things Canada has done for Great Britain at great expense in lives and great cost in food during a time when that nation was in crisis. We came to their rescue. Now, during a time of peace, we should be cementing that relationship. We should be building bridges of trade rather than tearing them down.
If there is any issue which has ever been brought up in this Parliament or in the British Parliament that relates to the previous days of the British Empire and the Commonwealth up to the present day, it is that of the fur trade. Let us ask our British friends tonight to reconsider this move and let us ask the general public in Great Britain and the animal lobbyists how they would feel if, all of a sudden, their very livelihood was cut out from underneath them. No matter what industry they work in, if suddenly tomorrow morning their work was no more, how would they feel? That is precisely what they are doing to many Canadians in this country today.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for letting me say these few words. I hope this debate in this Parliament of Canada tonight drives the message home to British parliamentarians.
